articles.title: Resetting the system
articles.content: THE issue of administrative restructuring is back on the political agenda. The interior minister hascalled for a referendumto seek public approval for the creation of new provinces, arguing that the existing system of governance has “collapsed” and needs a fundamental reset. In recent months, this contentious issue has been discussed at seminars and other public forums, while political leaders have voiced their individual opinions. The idea of holding a referendum on such a complex issue is apparently being floated to bypass the constitutional process. Coming from the interior minister, the proposal leaves little ambiguity about whose plan it is. Securing parliamentary approval for a referendum may not be difficult in a pliant house. But can a simple “yes” or “no” referendum resolve the intricate and politically sensitive question of creating new administrative units? There are certainly compelling reasons to restructure the existing provinces to improve governance. But the approach now being pursued is likely to open a Pandora’s box, creating chaos and further aggravating political instability. Several proposals for creating new administrative units may be circulating, but no political party has come forward with a concrete blueprint. While the PPP hasrejected any move to divide Sindhor create new administrative units in the province, the ruling PML-N has yet to adopt an official position, although individual ministers have expressed their views. There has been an intriguing silence on the issue from Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Nawaz Sharif. Not surprisingly, the smallercoalition partners, widely seen as close to the powers that be, have emerged as strong supporters of the restructuring plan, despite its contours remaining unclear. The question of administrative restructuring cannot be divorced from the broader democratic process. Mr Naqvi, himself a product of a system whose legitimacy remains contested, argues that a referendum is part of democracy. “We all talk about democracy. Parliamentarians represent the people of Pakistan. I request all political parties to consider that most survey reports suggest that new provinces should be created for better governance,” he maintains. Good governance requires rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountable institutions. Indeed, an elected parliament represents the will of the people and, in a democratic system, is the supreme legislative body mandated to initiate such changes. Yet, in this case, the debate on a major constitutional issue has not begun in parliament but has instead been initiated from outside it. Has there been any meaningful debate on this critical matter in the legislature, however contested its legitimacy? The interior minister’s appeal to political parties to take note of “survey reports” favouring the creation of new provinces is equally questionable. Opinion polls may offer some indication of public sentiment, but they cannot serve as the basis for constitutional change. Moreover, we know how limited in scope and reach many such surveys are in Pakistan. Has the minister also taken note of the numerous other surveys reflecting public dissatisfaction with the existing political order? More importantly, the Constitution clearly lays down the procedure for creating new provinces. The proposal for a referendum appears designed to circumvent these constitutional provisions. The Constitution also prescribes a well-defined procedure for its own amendment. There can be no shortcut to such a fundamental change. The 18th Amendment provides a useful example. It altered almost one-third of the Constitution, but only after nearly 18 months of intensive deliberations by a multiparty parliamentary committee, which eventually forged a consensus. Why cannot the same democratic and parliamentary process be followed for an issue of such national importance, rather than seeking to resolve it through a referendum? There is much talk about resetting a system of governance that has supposedly collapsed. There can be little disagreement that the country’s political and governance structures are deeply dysfunctional and require fundamental reform if Pakistan is to move forward. It is odd, however, that the rhetoric of resetting the system comes from those who are themselves equally responsible for its present state. Governance cannot be improved merely by creating new provinces. It requires, above all, a system founded on the rule of law, constitutional supremacy and accountable democratic institutions. Those now championing administrative restructuring and a reset are also responsible for undermining the democratic process and curtailing judicial independence through the 26th and27th Amendments, further eroding the Constitution’s fundamental principles. With democratic freedoms increasingly constrained, the country is moving towards authoritarianism. Creating new provinces or redrawing administrative boundaries will do little to improve governance or rescue a collapsing system in such circumstances. Phrases such as “resetting the system” and “referendum” are familiar instruments. Military rulers in the past have used similar language to consolidate their power and legitimise authoritarian rule. This time, too, the signs are hardly reassuring. The exercise looks less like a genuine attempt at reform and more like an effort to salvage a failing system through cosmetic adjustments. There has also been talk of a 28th Constitutional amendment. While the contours of the proposed amendment remain unclear, indications are that it could further tighten political control while incorporating administrative restructuring into a broader package of changes. This raises serious questions about the real objectives behind the proposed reforms. There is certainly an urgent need to break with the status quo and restore the democratic process. But that is not the kind of reset Mohsin Naqvi and others appear to be advocating. Neither a proposed referendum nor an impending 28th amendment, pursued outside a genuinely democratic process, is likely to bring political stability. What Pakistan needs is political stability built on constitutional supremacy, democratic freedoms and strong, independent institutions. Administrative restructuring may well be part of the solution, but it must emerge from an open, inclusive and constitutionally mandated democratic process — not be imposed from outside it.
articles.author: Zahid Hussain

articles.title: Predatory medicine
articles.content: “Medicine carries a morality that is destroyed when the emphasis is placed on the bottom line. Unless humanism and professionalism remain, medicine will become just another commodity in life’s marketplace.” — Dr William W. Parmley MEDICINE has traditionally been regarded as a profession founded on trust, compassion and an ethical commitment to heal. Patients entrust doctors with their bodies, their fears and, often, their lives. This relationship rests on an implicit promise: that medical decisions will be guided by the patient’s best interests. But what happens when the business of medicine begins to take precedence over the practice of medicine? In his book Predatory Medicine, US cardiologist Jack Vangrow draws attention to an uncomfortable reality: healthcare can become an extractive enterprise in which patients are exploited. He describes how both practitioners and institutions who should be protecting patients, instead exploit patients’ limited medical knowledge and trust. The commercialisation of medicine may not be inherently unethical. Private hospitals, clinics, labs and pharmaceutical firms have an important role in healthcare delivery. Medical innovation and research require investment, and healthcare professionals deserve fair remuneration. The problem arises when profit becomes the dominant consideration and the patient’s wellbeing becomes secondary. Healthcare is a rapidly expanding commercial market in a country where millions cannot afford basic treatment. Predatory medicine describes many practices that lead to profit-making: unnecessary investigations, excessive prescriptions, avoidable surgical procedures, inappropriate hospital admissions, inflated bills and the promotion of expensive treatments when cheaper, equally effective alternatives exist. The fundamental problem is the profound imbalance of knowledge and power between doctors and patients. Most patients cannot independently assess whether an investigation is necessary, whether a diagnosis is accurate or whether a proposed intervention offers meaningful benefit. They depend on their physician’s integrity and competence. When that trust is exploited, the consequences can be both financial and physical. Vangrow highlights the culture of professional complicity: doctors who recognise questionable practices but remain silent to protect their careers, professional relationships or financial interests. Predatory medicine, therefore, is not simply about a few unethical practitioners; it becomes embedded in the institutional culture. Vangrow’s observations are highly relevant for Pakistan, where private healthcare has become a hugely lucrative business, while a chronically underfunded public health system struggles to provide even basic services. The private medical sector continues to grow exponentially, with private hospitals, specialist clinics, diagnostic labs and pharmaceutical firms dominating healthcare delivery. According to Pakistan’s National Health Accounts 2021-22, total health expenditure stood at approximately Rs1.96 trillion, with the private sector accounting for 52.6 per cent. Much of this expenditure comes directly from household pockets. The World Bank’s latest available data show that out-of-pocket payments accounted for approximately 53pc of Pakistan’s current health expenditure in 2023. These figures illustrate the extent to which healthcare costs are transferred from the state to individual households. They also reveal a stark contradiction: healthcare is a rapidly expanding commercial market in a country where millions cannot afford basic treatment. Public health expenditure remains around one per cent of GDP, leaving government hospitals chronically under-resourced, overcrowded and struggling with shortages of medicines, equipment and personnel. While wealthier Pakistanis can access private healthcare, the poor have to suffer the indignity of treatment at government facilities, underscoring a deeply unequal healthcare system. A particular aspect of predatory medicine is to medicalise ordinary social problems, resulting in unnecessary lab tests, polypharmacy and doctor shopping. This is compounded by potential conflicts of interest involving pharmaceutical firms, labs, medical equipment suppliers and healthcare providers. Pakistan’s regulatory institutions — Provincial Healthcare Commissions (PHCs), PMDC and DRAP — have important responsibilities of licensing, quality assurance, professional conduct and patient safety. However, enforcement remains poor. Regulation must be more effective and independent. PHCs need resources and authority to monitor private hospitals and diagnostic facilities. Transparent disclosure of treatment costs, standardised billing, independent clinical audits and accessible patient complaint mechanisms are required. Addressing predatory medicine requires more than asking individual doctors to behave ethically. It requires changing the structures and incentives within which healthcare is practised. A functioning, adequately funded public health system is essential not only for providing services to those who cannot afford private treatment but also for preventing the private sector from becoming the only realistic option for millions. Financial relationships between doctors, pharmaceutical firms, labs and hospitals should be disclosed and appropriately regulated. Clinical decisions must be based on evidence and patient need, not commercial incentives. Medical education must place greater emphasis on professional ethics, the social responsibilities of medicine and the doctor-patient relationship. Being a good doctor is not simply about diagnostic accuracy or technical competence; it is also about recognising vulnerability, avoiding unnecessary interventions and respecting patients’ autonomy. Healthcare is not like any other commodity and a patient seeking treatment is not an ordinary consumer making a purchase in a competitive marketplace. Illness creates vulnerability, distress, dependence and desperation. The relationship between a doctor and patient cannot be driven by market principles. In Pakistan, the ethical foundations of medical practice receive insufficient attention. We may have internationally accredited hospitals and specialists, yet still fail in our obligation to provide equitable and compassionate care. The purpose of medicine is to heal, relieve suffering and protect human dignity. When profit displaces these obligations, medicine becomes predatory. We not only need more hospitals and better technology, but also a commitment to the ethics and social responsibility that should define the medical profession. The writer is professor emeritus of psychiatry, Aga Khan University.
articles.author: Murad Moosa Khan

articles.title: Not another Yalta
articles.content: WHEN the leaders of the USSR, US and UK gathered at a Crimean resort in Feb 1945 for a weeklong trilateral summit, an extensive agenda awaited them. With the Nazis caught in a pincer movement between the rapidly advancing Red Army and its western allies, the European segment of the world war had entered its endgame. The architecture of peace needed to be sketched out. Historians still argue about whether Franklin Roosevelt and Winston Churchill conceded too much to Joseph Stalin in delineating ‘spheres of influence’, but it was indisputably a momentous occasion. For better or worse, many of the decisions made at Yalta endured for decades, and some still resonate. No comparable outcome can be imagined from this week’s summit in Shenzhen. It may well turn out to be little more than a grandiose photo-op. A domineering presence on the global stage has additional appeal for Donald Trump following his domestichumiliation in the midterm elections. Vladimir Putin is inevitably keen to be counted among the ‘Big 3’. By many accounts, Xi Jinping is a reluctant host — perhaps partly because there’s only a vague agenda — “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations”, according to Beijing. And he’s naturally wary of Trump’s tendency to grandstand. The Iran war could figure in discussions at Shenzhen. The Iran war is expected to figure in the discussions. Some good could possibly come out of that if both Xi and Putin urge the US president to recognise the error of his ways. The conflict is particularly painful for China, given its reliance on Iranian crude. On the brighter side, China’s oil imports have decreased by design, while exports of its cutting-edge green tech — including solar panels — have substantially increased. Russia, on the other hand, has been delighted by asanctions reprieveand a surge in petroleum exports, largely due to the transport hiatus in the Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab straits. Besides, the US/Israeli conflict helps Russia portray its war against Ukraine as a comparable venture aimed at safeguarding its security. Moscow’s stance makes slightly more sense than the justifications from Washington and Tel Aviv for their aggression against Iran. China sees both wars as huge strategic errors. Trump seems to believe the Israeli propaganda that Tehran must be prevented from acquiring a nuclear weapon, an outcome that now logically seems likelier than it did before the attacks. That may help to explain why nuclear proliferation was among the topics he hoped to broach at his talks with Xi and Putin. Back in February, his administration turned down Moscow’s proposal to extend a strategic arms reduction treaty, with Trump aspiring for a new deal that includes China, whose expanding nuclear arsenal appears to have alarmed Sinophobes in the US. Given that even its projected stockpiles are a fraction of what’s stored in Russian and American silos, Beijing does not wish to play ball. Shortly before flying to Asia, Trump noted that denuclearisation, Iran, economics, trade and “my favourite topic, Ukraine” would be up for discussion. Volodymyr Zelensky is alarmed by the possibilities, but a carve-up without Kyiv at the table is hardly likely. China sees Ukraine as a European issue that should be discussed at a more appropriate forum. Trump is disinclined, meanwhile, to bring up theNvidia fiascoafter the US chip-maker’s CEO Jensen Huang was ousted over revelations about an affair with a purported Chinese ‘asset’. America remains determined to deny China superiority in artificial intelligence through curbs on chip exports. But that’s probably another lost battle. Exactly what the three leaders will talk about remains to be seen. Climate change won’t be on the agenda. That’s being thrashed out at COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, where there’s no official US representation, given the Trump administration’s focus on exacerbating global heating despite rapidly mounting evidence about its catastrophic consequences, from the devastation in Nepal caused by glacier collapse to an estimated 50,000 heatwave deaths in Europe during a scorching summer, not to mention the ecocidal aspect of the Palestinian genocide as well as the Iranian, Ukrainian and Sudanese conflicts. Not to mention the ginormous carbon footprint of proliferating US data centres. As Swedish activist Greta Thunberg accurately spelt it out in Antalya, “The planet is not dying, it is being killed.” And the outgoing UN Secretary-General, Antonio Guterres, was equally correct in pointing out: “It’s make or bake time.” He might have erred, though, in comparing fossil fuels to dinosaurs and claiming the latter “did not have a lobby”. They do, and some of its components might be congregating in Shenzhen right now.
articles.author: Mahir Ali

articles.title: One light day
articles.content: ON Nov 18, 2026 (today), the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (Nasa) spacecraft, Voyager 1, the furthest travelled human-made object, launched in 1977 and since then travelling at a non-stop average speed of 61,200km per hour, willcover a distanceof one light day. In Cosmos, astronomer Carl Sagan writes, “The dimensions of the cosmos are so large that using familiar units of distance, such as meters or miles, chosen for their utility on earth, would make little sense. Instead, we measure distance with the speed of light [ie the distance light travels in one year]”. Light travels at the superluminal speed of 1,079,252,848km/h, and thus is capable of orbiting the earth’s equator 7.5 times in one second. A Boeing 747, travelling at non-stop cruising speed, which is around 900km/h, would take around 3,300 years to cover a distance of one light day, and reach where Voyager 1 will be today. For the feat, you would have had to take off in a Boeing 747 in the Bronze Age, when Rameses II was ruling Egypt, and travel continuously at cruising speed to cover a distance of one light day by 2026. Your journey would have had to commence in a world before Christ, Cyrus, Caesar and Confucius. While a light day seems very far, on the cosmic scale, it is mundanely trivial. Our nearest star, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away. A journey Voyager 1 — according to Nasa — is expected to cover in 75,000 years, despite its hypersonic speed. Imagine what lies beyond the gaze of the naked eye. To fathom the stupefying distances, Richard Dawkins in The Magic of Reality writes, “Go out into a big field with a football and plonk it down to represent the sun [which is 1.3 million times larger than the earth in volume]. Then walk 25 metres away and drop a peppercorn to represent the Earth’s size and its distance from the sun. The moon, to the same scale, would be a pinhead, and it would be only 5 centimetres away from the peppercorn. But the nearest other star, Proxima Centauri, to the same scale, would be another (slightly smaller) football, located about six-and-a-half thousand kilometres away”. That is about the same distance from London to Chicago. We naively believe that when we gaze up into the night sky, we witness billions upon billions of stars — and perceive this as infinity. The actual number is close to 6,000, with the furthermost stars visible to the naked eye being posited no further than 15,000 light-years away. Imagine what lies beyond the gaze of the naked eye. The Milky Way galaxy, with its 100 to 400 billion stars, is estimated by Nasa to be 100,000 light-years across. Our solar system, situated about 27,000 light years from the galactic centre of the Milky Way hosting the super-giant black hole, Sagittarius A*, and orbiting it at a rate of 828,000 km/h, takes approximately 230m years to complete one galactic year. The last time our solar system was where it is now, dinosaurs had just begun to appear. In The Princeton Field Guide to Dinosaurs, Gregory S. Paul writes, “Only one galactic year ago the dinosaurs had just appeared on planet earth. When dinosaurs first appeared, our solar system was already well over 4 billion years old, and 95 per cent of the history of our planet had already passed”. Our nearest galaxy, the Andromeda galaxy with its one trillion stars, is around 2.5m light years away, what to say of the other two trillion galaxies which are spread across an observable universe with a diameter 93bn light-years across. Stephen Hawking illuminates in A Brief History of Time how Edwin Hubble’s discoveries in 1929 led to “the landmark observation that wherever you look, distant galaxies are moving rapidly away from us. In other words, the universe is expanding”. Accordingly, the further galaxies are, the faster they recede, sometimes faster than the speed of light. Though nothing can travel faster than the speed of light, space can expand faster. The inference — even if we were miraculously able to travel at the speed of light, there would be parts of the universe which would be perpetually beyond our reach. We, homo sapiens, whom paleoanthropologists believe appeared 300,000 years ago, seldom view our own insignificance from this cosmic perspective. If we did, it would rob us of our prejudices, partialities and pre-conceptions. In his essay Wonder and Skepticism, Carl Sagan writes, “The truth may be puzzling. It may take some work to grapple with. It may be counterintuitive. It may contradict deeply held prejudices. It may not be consonant with what we desperately want to be true. But our preferences do not determine what’s true”. Voyager 1’s feat of travelling one light day should be a moment of pride and humility for the whole of humanity.
articles.author: Asad-ul-Mulk

articles.title: Untenable stalemate
articles.content: NEARLY nine months into a conflict of choice that has rattled economies from Europe to Asia, there seem to be few agreeable options for the US where ending the Iran war is concerned. No one — perhaps apart from Israel and some hawks in Washington — wants an escalation, while coming to an agreement on Iran’s terms would result in considerable embarrassment for Donald Trump. However, Pakistan, which has played a crucial mediatory role in the conflict, and other regional states still have expectations that a negotiated settlement can be reached. As Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar told the ECO meeting on Monday, “we have not given up hope” for peace. The Iranian foreign minister was also in Islamabad for the event, and praised Pakistan’s efforts to broker peace. But the most sincere efforts by Pakistan or any other mediator will not bear fruit unless there is clarity in Washington. President Trump, as has been his practice, has oscillated between saying the war is “effectively over”, and threatening fresh strikes if talks fall through. This cognitive dissonance must end. Over the past few days, there have been some low-key military engagements between the US and Iran. The US had reportedly attacked facilities on the Iranian coast, while Tehran hit back by targeting American sites in Bahrain. These exchanges have the potential to get out of hand and spark a bigger confrontation. Which is why the quicker the matter is resolved, the better. The collective voice from the states of this region is clearly against war, while the majority of the American people also appear uninterested in fresh clashes with Iran. Therefore, it is time the White House faced the bitter reality that its ill-conceived Iran campaign — fuelled by bad Israeli advice — has failed, and committed to resolving the imbroglio peacefully. The option of attacking Iran again must be taken off the table by the US. In fact, there should be a positive response to the Iranian proposal currently on the table, specifically where lifting the blockade, ending sanctions, and allowing access to Tehran’s funds goes. This may seem like ‘capitulation’ to Mr Trump, but these matters should have been thought through before launching this disastrous war. Tehran should also show flexibility, particularly where free and unhindered access through the Strait of Hormuz is concerned. Should Washington opt for the diplomatic off-ramp, it will find that regional states, particularly Pakistan, Qatar and others, will be happy to facilitate dialogue. However, indecision and a damaging status quo that is affecting regional peace and the global economy cannot be allowed to continue. It is time the Trump administration did the right thing.
articles.author: Editorial

articles.title: Poor treatment
articles.content: IT is unseemly that a jailed political leader is forced to beseech the chief justices of the Federal Constitutional Court, the Supreme Court and the Islamabad High Court for medical attention. In anopen letterissued Monday, former prime minister Imran Khan detailed his and his wife’s medical condition, claiming he faces heightened risk of brain haemorrhage while his spouse could lose her eyesight. “I will only remain able to prove my innocence if I stay alive. I appeal to your Lordships, on the most basic grounds of human compassion: give me justice before it is too late,” reads his letter, penned on his behalf by his lawyer, Salman Safdar. The government still disputes this, and insists that the two continue to receive adequate medical attention. In fact, Parliamentary Affairs Minister Tariq Fazal Chaudhry, responding to the letter, said Mr Khan is “[…] among the most privileged prisoners in Pakistan,” while telling the PTI to stop “politicising his health”. But even if government ministers believe the former PM is embellishing the facts, what is the harm in allowing him a medical examination under the supervision of his physicians, as theSC directed in August? Some may argue that the many difficulties Mr Khan finds himself in are self-created. There are many in the ruling dispensation who believe that what is being done to him is ‘justice’, considering that he, too, had victimised his opponents during his time in power. Mr Khan’s speeches about depriving his jailed political opponents of various facilities and amenities granted to them have not been forgotten in those circles. Still, as far as Mr Khan and his wife’s health is concerned, the government must show compassion, if not respect for their rights. The courts have given the state grounds to deprive Mr Khan and his spouse of their liberty, not their health. If the two prisoners are complaining that their treatment has not been adequate, the government can allow those needs to be met to their satisfaction without making any change to their status as prisoners. There is no conceivable harm in making such an allowance. Those in power today should also think about the precedent they are setting. Do they want to be treated similarly in the future? The cycle of revenge needs to stop, and compassion alone can break it.
articles.author: Editorial
